title: The Tofu Shop Comes Down
part: PART FOUR: THE NIGHT OF THE NORTH WIND

pages.text:
*The Owl Alley Sheet, No. 17. Today's news: a tofu shop was sacrificed for a street.*

Captain Daigoro did not shout. He did not need to. The wind was doing the shouting for him, tearing at the hem of his leather hood and snapping the paper tassels on his pole. He stood in the middle of the road, his square face grim, and pointed his thick finger at the tofu shop.

The shop was narrow, tight against the bathhouse wall. It stood between the fire and the rest of Owl Alley. It was a wall of wood, and wood was the fire’s best friend.

Umekichi stood on the other side of the street, his white headband askew, his huge forearms hanging loose at his sides. Osen clutched a heavy pot of broth to her chest, her face pale as the steam rising from it. Behind them, the rest of the alley watched, their breath pluming in the cold air.

Daigoro walked toward the tofu maker. The crowd parted. He stopped an arm’s length away and placed a heavy hand on Umekichi’s shoulder. He looked at the man, then back at the shop.

"Umekichi," he said, his voice low and rough. "It has to go. Now."

Umekichi looked at his shop. He looked at the window where he had ground the soybeans for twenty years. He looked at the door where he had hung his lucky charm, now hidden by soot. He swallowed. His throat worked once, twice.

"Do it," he said.
pages.image: Captain Daigoro in a black-trimmed leather firefighter coat places a hand on the shoulder of Umekichi, a large man in a white apron and headband, while Osen clutches a pot behind him, the wooden tofu shop glowing with orange fire in the dark alley background.

pages.text:
The sound was not a crash. It was a long, thundering groan of timber snapping and sliding. The tofu shop did not fall so much as fold, crumbling in on itself like a wet paper crane. Dust billowed up, grey and thick, rolling over the road to settle on the shoulders of the firefighters.

The hooks swung. The ropes pulled. With every tug, the wall shuddered. With every snap, the fire screamed. Then, with a final, heavy thud, the roof caved in. The gap between the bathhouse and the rest of the alley was empty. It became a wide, dark mouth of cold air and ash.

The flames reached the edge. They licked at the nothing there, spat and hissed, but could not cross. They had no wood to eat. The wind, which had been howling, seemed to pause. It dropped a fraction, a small, tired sigh, as if the effort of blowing sparks across that gap had exhausted it.

By the time the temple bell rang the morning, the alley was standing. It was grey. It was steaming. It was safe. The bathhouse stood as a black skeleton of beams. The tofu shop lay in a pile of splintered planks. But the print shop, the noodle stall, and the homes remained. Not one person was hurt.
pages.image: A wide gap of dark ash and splintered wood separates a blackened bathhouse roof frame from a row of intact low wooden houses with grey tiled roofs and paper windows, grey steam rising from the cold empty earth street in the early morning light.

pages.text:
Dawn broke over the alley in shades of wet slate and pale gold. The road was slick with ash and melted snow. The neighbors gathered, not in a crowd, but in a loose circle, their breath mixing with the steam that rose from the ruined bathhouse.

Okiku was first. She had wheeled her cart, miraculously unscathed, to the center of the road. She ladled hot broth into bowls, passing them hand to hand. No one spoke. No one asked for money. The broth was thick with ginger and green onions, and it smelled like life.

Mother Okiyo stood beside her, holding a bundle of cloth. She untied it and began to pass out rice balls, small and neat, wrapped in leaves. Haru watched them take them, her hands trembling slightly as she accepted one.

Umekichi sat on the edge of the pile of planks that had been his shop. He did not move. In his lap, he held a tofu mold, the wooden frame with the cloth inside. He stroked it with his thumb, over and over, a quiet, repetitive motion. He looked at the mold. He looked at the empty space where the shop had been. He did not weep. He just held it, as if he were holding the last piece of something precious.
pages.image: Umekichi sits on a pile of splintered wood in the morning mist, holding a rectangular wooden tofu mold in his lap, while Okiku in a faded pink jacket ladles broth into bowls for neighbors standing in a loose circle nearby.

pages.text:
Haru sat on the wooden bridge rail, her legs dangling over the canal. The water below was dark and still, reflecting the grey sky. In her lap lay her booklet, the pages soft and grubby from use. Her fingers were stained with ink, a deep black smudge that would not wash out for days.

She opened the booklet. She uncapped her brush. Her hand shook, just once, and then it stilled. She began to write. The letters were small, careful, precise. She did not write about the roar. She did not write about the fear. She wrote about the spark.

She wrote about the pile of cherry-wood shavings near the bathhouse furnace. She wrote about the cracked chimney cap, the hairline fracture she had noticed three days ago when the wind was rising. She wrote about the north wind, the dry, relentless wind that had blown for three days straight. She wrote about the shavings, how they had caught the spark, how they had caught fire, how the fire had climbed.

It was true. Every word was true. She looked at the page, at the black strokes drying on the paper. The smell of ink was sharp and clean, cutting through the smell of ash.

"I will print this," she whispered to the empty air. "I will print it today."
pages.image: Haru, an eleven-year-old girl in a rust-orange kimono with a vermilion cord in her topknot, sits on a wooden bridge rail over a dark canal, writing carefully in a small folded-paper booklet with a brush, her expression serious and focused.

pages.text:
The voice started low, then rose. It cracked with the early morning cold, but it carried. It was a big voice, round and loud, the kind that could be heard from the other end of the alley.

Haru froze. Her brush hovered over the page, a drop of ink trembling at the tip.

It was Bunta. The seller was standing in the middle of the road, his deep straw hat pulled low, a fan in his other hand. He was reading from a sheet of paper, a fresh sheet, the ink still wet and glossy.

"Listen well, good people!" Bunta boomed. "The Turtle House has a story for you today! A story of a fire! A story of a blame! Listen to the words, for they are the words of the Turtle House!"

The crowd turned. The sound of feet shuffling on the wet road filled the air. Haru looked down at her booklet, then up at Bunta, who was waving the sheet high above his head. The paper fluttered in the wind, a white flag of something she had not yet expected.
pages.image: Bunta, a large man in an indigo-and-white striped kimono and a deep straw hat, stands in the middle of an ash-covered street holding a blank white paper sheet high above his head, while Haru watches from the background with a shocked expression.
